source_refs.note: Negative Feedback: a main subheading of 13.1.2 Feedback Mechanisms, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 2-3.

blocks.text: A negative feedback system is a mechanism in which the output or product of a system reduces the activity of the system. It is the most common form of regulation. Common examples of negative feedback include the regulation of body temperature, blood glucose levels, and hormone secretion.

For example, if body temperature exceeds the set point of 37°C, the thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus of brain detect this change. They send signals to the control centre (thermoregulator in hypothalamus). The control centre sends messages to effectors (e.g., sweat glands). The effectors respond by producing sweat which lowers the temperature. The output of this process (lowering of temperature to the set point) influences the thermoreceptors negatively. As a result, the thermoreceptors stop sending message to the control centre.

blocks.alt: Flowchart from top to bottom: Heat; body temperature rises; Thermoreceptor (area in hypothalamus), marked Receptors; Thermoregulator (area in hypothalamus), marked Control centre; Sweat glands, marked Effector; Sweating; body temperature falls. A dashed line labelled 'Negative feedback' with a minus sign runs from the fallen body temperature back to the thermoreceptor, with the words 'Stop sending signals to control centre'.
